Because polite reasoning had failed to bring about change for so long, he believes only fierce criticism will actually wake the country up.

Douglass explains that the Fourth of July only reminds enslaved people of their ongoing suffering, calling the nation's celebrations a "hollow mockery" because boasting about freedom while people are held in chains is an insult. He also labels the festivities a "thin veil to cover up crimes," meaning that religious parades and patriotic speeches are just used to hide the bloody horrors of slavery. To an enslaved person, the holiday is simply painful proof that the nation does not treat them as equals.

Writing right before the Revolutionary War, Patrick Henry saw liberty as political independence from Great Britain, warning the colonists that British troops were sent to "bind and rivet upon us those chains" of tyranny. In contrast, Douglass spoke in 1852 when America was already an established country, meaning liberty to him was the literal freedom of Black Americans from "gross injustice and cruelty." Henry wanted white colonists to break away from an overseas king, while Douglass wanted the United States to fulfill its founding promise for the millions of people it still held in bondage.
